title: Pressure ulcer prevention and categorisation
blurb: Assess risk, check skin (including darker skin tones), prevent pressure damage and categorise ulcers correctly.
question: Mrs Adeyemi, 78, has dark brown skin and has been in bed since a stroke. Over her sacrum the skin is intact but feels warmer and firmer than the surrounding area, and she says it is sore. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: A pressure ulcer is localised damage to the skin and/or underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence or related to a medical or other device, caused by sustained pressure, including pressure combined with shear. In plain English: when weight or a device presses on the same spot for too long, blood cannot reach the tissue and it breaks down. Most are preventable with risk assessment, skin checks and regular movement.

teach.caption: National Wound Care Strategy Programme (NWCSP) 2024: use the aSSKINg framework to plan individual care for anyone at risk.

head: Point
Guidance
rows: On admission to hospital or care home (NWCSP: within 6 hours)
Validated tool to support judgement, e.g. PURPOSE-T, Braden, Waterlow
teach.caption: NICE CG179 recs 1.1.2–1.1.4, 1.1.8–1.1.9, 1.2.6; NWCSP Pressure Ulcer Recommendations (May 2024).

teach.h: Checking skin, including darker skin tones
teach.body: Test redness for blanching with finger pressure (press for about 3 seconds) or a clear disc (diascopy). Redness that blanches is reactive hyperaemia and should fade in 20 to 30 minutes off the area. In darker skin, redness may not show: look for persistent purple, blue or darker hues and feel for warmth, coolness, firmness or bogginess, and ask about pain or itching. If there is non-blanching erythema, start prevention and recheck the skin at least every 2 hours until it resolves.
teach.cite: NICE CG179 recs 1.1.5–1.1.7; NWCSP Categorisation Tool 2024

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Adeyemi after her stroke
teach.body: The warm, firm, sore area over Mrs Adeyemi's sacrum is a warning even though the skin looks intact: in dark skin, erythema may not be visible. The nurse documents the findings, starts preventive care (high-specification foam mattress, repositioning at least every 4 hours as she is at high risk, heels offloaded, continence and nutrition reviewed) and rechecks the skin at least every 2 hours until resolved, escalating to tissue viability if it worsens.

teach.caption: From EPUAP/NPIAP/PPPIA 2019 via the NWCSP Categorisation Tool 2024. A wound whose base is hidden by slough or eschar (formerly 'unstageable') is recorded initially as Category 3 and re-categorised if debridement shows Category 4.

children.edge: Over bone or under a device
children.label: Pressure ulcer

children.edge: Diffuse, shiny, from urine or faeces
children.label: Moisture-associated skin damage

teach.caption: NWCSP 2024 and NHS Improvement 2018. Where pressure and moisture combine over a pressure point, classify as a pressure ulcer.

teach.h: Things NICE CG179 says not to do
items: Do not offer skin massage or rubbing to prevent pressure ulcers.
Do not use a standard-specification foam mattress for an adult with a pressure ulcer.
Do not give nutritional supplements solely to prevent pressure ulcers if intake is adequate.
Do not give systemic antibiotics just because a swab is positive with no clinical signs of infection.
Do not routinely use topical antiseptics or antimicrobials on pressure ulcers.

teach.text: Blanching redness that fades is not Category 1. Category 1 is non-blanching. And in darker skin tones, absence of visible redness is not reassurance: feel for warmth, firmness and ask about pain. The older 'unstageable' and 'deep tissue injury' labels are no longer used as categories in England (NWCSP 2024).

items: Assess risk on admission (NWCSP: within 6 hours) and when condition changes; tools support judgement.
Reposition adults at risk at least 6-hourly, high risk at least 4-hourly; children at least 4-hourly.
Blanch test by finger or clear disc; non-blanching = prevention plus 2-hourly skin checks.
Categories 1–4; slough-covered base recorded as Category 3 at first; MASD and mucosal ulcers not categorised.
High-specification foam mattress, heel offloading, no massage, no routine supplements or antibiotics.

summary: You can now assess pressure ulcer risk, check skin for blanching in all skin tones and plan aSSKINg prevention with the right repositioning intervals. You can also categorise damage using the four NWCSP categories and tell pressure ulcers apart from moisture damage.

A.q: Mr Hollis, 82, is admitted to a medical ward after a fall. He has limited mobility and had a pressure ulcer last year. Under NICE CG179, when should his pressure ulcer risk be assessed?
options: Within 24 hours of transfer to the ward
Once he has been on bed rest for 2 days
When the skin first shows any redness
A.why: NICE CG179: assess and document pressure ulcer risk on admission to secondary care. NWCSP 2024 sets a 6-hour window from admission.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is too late; the NWCSP standard is within 6 hours of admission.
whyNot.1: Waiting for prolonged bed rest misses early prevention.
whyNot.3: Redness means damage may already be starting; risk assessment comes first.

A.q: Mrs Ford, 74, has had a stroke and cannot reposition herself. She is incontinent and assessed as high risk of pressure ulcers. How often should she be repositioned at minimum?
A.why: NICE CG179: adults at high risk should change position at least every 4 hours, with help if they cannot do it themselves.

whyNot.0: 2-hourly is the skin reassessment interval for non-blanching erythema, not the CG179 repositioning minimum.
whyNot.2: At least every 6 hours is for adults at risk, not high risk.

A.q: Mr Kerr, 79, has a red area over his heel. The nurse wants to check whether it blanches. Which method is recommended?
options: Rubbing the area gently to see if colour returns
Measuring the area with a paper wound ruler
Finger pressure or a clear disc over the area
Comparing it with a photograph taken last week
A.why: NICE CG179 and NWCSP: use finger palpation (about 3 seconds) or diascopy with a transparent disc to test for blanching.

whyNot.0: Rubbing or massage is advised against and can damage tissue.
whyNot.1: Measuring records size but does not test blanching.
whyNot.3: A photograph helps track change but cannot test blanching.

B.q: Mrs Doyle, 81, is incontinent of urine. On her buttocks the nurse finds diffuse, shiny red areas with superficial skin loss, not over a bony prominence and with no pressure history. How should this be recorded?
B.why: Diffuse damage caused by urine, away from bony prominences and without pressure, is moisture-associated skin damage (an irritant dermatitis). It is not categorised as a pressure ulcer; use barrier preparations.

whyNot.1: Category 2 is partial-thickness loss caused by pressure, usually over a bony prominence.
whyNot.2: Category 1 is localised non-blanching discolouration from pressure, with intact skin.
whyNot.3: There is no medical device involved.

B.q: Mr Mensah, 85, has a sacral wound with full-thickness skin loss. Fat is visible, but no bone, tendon or muscle. How should it be categorised?
B.why: Category 3 is full-thickness skin loss into subcutaneous tissue, without exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone (NWCSP 2024).

whyNot.0: Category 2 is partial-thickness loss, not into fat.
whyNot.1: Category 4 has exposed or palpable bone, tendon or muscle.

B.q: Mr Burke, 70, is well nourished and at high risk of pressure ulcers. His wife asks whether a supplement drink or a daily massage of his heels would help prevent them. What is the best answer?
options: Both would help and should be added to his written care plan
The massage would help, but the supplement would not
Neither is advised; repositioning and heel offloading are
The supplement would help, but the massage would not
B.why: NICE CG179: do not offer massage or rubbing, and do not offer supplements solely to prevent pressure ulcers if intake is adequate. Repositioning and heel offloading are recommended.

whyNot.0: CG179 advises against both in this situation.
whyNot.1: Massage is advised against as it may damage tissue.
whyNot.3: Supplements are not advised for prevention when intake is already adequate.

C.q: Mr Walsh, 77, has a heel wound covered in black eschar, so the wound base cannot be seen. How should this be recorded under current NWCSP guidance in England?
options: As a suspected deep tissue injury
As unstageable until the black eschar has separated
As Category 3 at first, reviewed after debridement
As Category 2 until the depth is confirmed
C.why: NWCSP (2024): wounds with broken skin whose base is hidden by slough or necrosis, formerly 'unstageable', are recorded initially as Category 3 and re-categorised if debridement reveals Category 4.

whyNot.0: Deep tissue injury is no longer a reporting category, and this skin is not intact.
whyNot.1: 'Unstageable' has been removed as a category in the NWCSP recommendations.
whyNot.3: Category 2 is partial thickness, which underestimates necrotic full-thickness damage.

C.q: Ms Ruiz, 60, has a nasogastric tube. The nurse notices a small open area on the inside of her nostril where the tube presses. How should this be recorded?
options: As a Category 2 device-related pressure ulcer
As a mucosal pressure ulcer, not categorised
As a Category 1 pressure ulcer of the nose
As moisture-associated skin damage of the nose
C.why: NWCSP 2024: pressure ulcers on mucous membranes cannot be categorised because the tissue lacks skin layers; record them as mucosal pressure ulcers with device details.

whyNot.0: Device-related ulcers on skin are categorised, but mucosal ones are not.
whyNot.2: Category 1 describes intact skin, and mucosa is not categorised.
whyNot.3: The damage is from tube pressure, not moisture.

C.q: Mrs Lee, 88, at high risk, has non-blanching erythema over her sacrum on a high-specification foam mattress. She is repositioned 4-hourly. Which addition is most appropriate?
options: Recheck her skin at least every 2 hours until it resolves
Massage the area at each turn to improve local circulation
Apply a topical antiseptic to the area to prevent infection
Start oral supplements to help the skin heal more quickly
C.why: NICE CG179: in adults with non-blanching erythema, start preventive action and consider repeating the skin assessment at least every 2 hours until resolved.

whyNot.1: Massage is advised against and may worsen damage.
whyNot.2: Topical antiseptics are not routinely used and the skin is intact.
whyNot.3: Supplements are not advised solely for prevention if intake is adequate.

reteach.title: Pressure plus time
reteach.question: Why does sitting still for a few minutes do no harm, but lying still for hours can break the skin?

blocks.h: It is the duration that does the damage
blocks.body: Pressure squeezes small blood vessels shut. Healthy people shift without thinking, so the tissue refills with blood. People who cannot feel, move or understand (after a stroke, under sedation, with dementia) stay still, so the tissue starves. That is why prevention is about moving people often enough, spreading their weight on the right surface and checking the skin at the bony points.

blocks.text: The repositioning intervals in CG179 are minimums ('at least every 6 hours', 'at least every 4 hours'). Many people need moving more often; document the frequency each person needs.

explain.body: Assess on admission (NWCSP: within 6 hours) and when status changes. Use a validated tool (PURPOSE-T, Braden, Waterlow) to support, not replace, clinical judgement. Risk factors include limited mobility, loss of sensation, previous ulcer, poor nutrition, inability to reposition and cognitive impairment.

items.label: NWCSP risk assessment window after admission

test.q: Which tool does the NWCSP recommend for pressure ulcer risk assessment?
test.why: NWCSP 2024: screen with PURPOSE-T or another validated tool containing at least the same risk factors.

explain.body: Adults at risk: at least every 6 hours. Adults at high risk: at least every 4 hours. Children and young people at risk: at least every 4 hours. Help those who cannot move themselves, with equipment, and document the frequency.

test.q: An adult assessed as at risk (not high risk) should change position at least how often?
test.why: NICE CG179: adults at risk should change position at least every 6 hours.

whyNot.0: 2 hours is the skin recheck interval for non-blanching erythema.
whyNot.2: 4 hours is for high risk adults and for children at risk.

explain.body: Blanch test with a finger for about 3 seconds or a clear disc. Darker skin: look for persistent red, blue or purple hues; feel temperature and firmness; ask about pain. Non-blanching: prevention plus skin checks at least every 2 hours.

test.q: Healthy reactive redness should fade within about how long once pressure is relieved?
test.why: NWCSP 2024: reactive hyperaemia should resolve after a short period, 20 to 30 minutes.

whyNot.1: Redness lasting hours suggests damage, not normal reactive hyperaemia.
whyNot.2: 6–8 hours is far beyond the normal response.
whyNot.3: Persistent redness for a day indicates damage.

explain.body: Category 1: intact, non-blanching. Category 2: partial-thickness loss or blister. Category 3: full-thickness into fat. Category 4: bone, tendon or muscle exposed or palpable. Hidden base: Category 3 at first. Mucosal ulcers and MASD are not categorised.

test.q: A sacral wound shows a shallow open area with a pink wound bed and no slough. Which category is it?
test.why: Category 2: partial-thickness skin loss involving epidermis and/or dermis, such as a shallow open ulcer or blister.

whyNot.1: Category 3 is full-thickness loss into fat.
whyNot.3: Category 4 exposes bone, tendon or muscle.
